PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Clean surroundings give us clear things to talk about. In this sub-strand you will say the sounds /ʌ/ and /ɔː/ and the clusters br, sw, pr, cl and gr in words such as brush, water, broom, sweep, protect, clear and grass. You will speak at a steady speed, use gestures, and give a short speech about the environment.

## Strand 12.0: Clean Environment
Sub-strand 12.1.1: Listening and Speaking: Pronunciation and Vocabulary
Suggested lessons: 2

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) speak accurately, with expression and at the right speed (minimal hesitation) for fluency
b) use nonverbal cues appropriately for self- expression
c) use vocabulary related to the theme in a variety of contexts
d) promote the importance of fluency in speech

## What this sub-strand covers
• Speaking Fluency

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should you speak at the right speed?
2. How can one pass a message without using words?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This iss achieved as the learner makes short speeches in collaboration with peers.
• Creativity and Imagination: The learner creatively composes a speech on clean environment and delivers it fluently to the peers.

## Values
• Respect is nurtured as the learner respects the peers’ opinions when reciting poems collaboratively.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social Cohesion and integrity are enhanced as the learner engages with peers in doing activities such as reciting poems and making short speeches.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to link fluency in speaking to all learning areas as fluency is required when making presentations.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 12.0 Clean Environment, Sub-strand 12.1.1 Pronunciation and Vocabulary

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Sounds, clusters and environment words

LESSON 1: SOUNDS, CLUSTERS AND ENVIRONMENT WORDS
================================================

## What you will learn
• Say /ʌ/, /ɔː/ and the clusters br, sw, pr, cl and gr clearly.
• Pick those words out of a short oral text.
• Ask and answer yes or no questions about a clean environment.

Curriculum outcomes: a) speak accurately, with expression and at the right speed (minimal hesitation) for fluency; c) use vocabulary related to the theme in a variety of contexts

## Introduction
Say cup, then say water. The first vowel is short and open. The second is longer and made with rounded lips. Environment talk uses both, often beside clusters such as br in broom and gr in grass.

## Notes
### The short sound /ʌ/
Open your mouth a little and keep the sound short. You hear it in cup, up, sun, cut, brush, rubbish, mud and dump. It is the vowel in the first part of the word rubbish. Do not stretch it into the long sound in food.

The word bush is different. A bush is a small woody plant, and its vowel is the short sound in put, not the sound in cup. Learn bush as a meaning word, and practise /ʌ/ with rubbish and brush.

### The long sound /ɔː/
Round your lips and hold the sound. You hear it in water, lawn, walk, saw, tall, all, floor and door. We walk across the lawn to fetch water. Do not cut the sound short, or water can be hard to recognise.

### Consonant clusters
Say the two consonants together, with no vowel between them.

- br: broom, brush, branch, bring
- sw: sweep, swim, swing
- pr: protect, proud, promise
- cl: clean, clear, class
- gr: grass, green, grow, ground

A broom sweeps. A brush scrubs. We protect rivers and trees. We clear a drain so that water can pass. Green grass grows when we care for the soil.

### Other useful words
The compound is the open ground around a home or school. A bin holds rubbish. A rubbish pit is a hole used for waste that can rot. A drain carries water away. A neighbourhood is the area around your home. Hills, rivers and trees are part of the environment. Cleanliness means keeping that environment clean. To conserve water means to use it carefully and not waste it.

### An oral text
Listen for the target sounds: 'Bring a broom and a brush. Sweep the rubbish off the lawn, then clear the drain so the water can run. Protect the young trees and let the grass grow.'

### Yes or no questions
A yes or no question can be answered with yes or no, often plus a short verb.

Do you sweep the compound? Yes, I do. / No, I do not.
Is the drain clear? Yes, it is. / No, it is not.
Can we protect the river? Yes, we can.

Speak the question as a whole, not one word at a time. Your voice usually rises a little at the end.

## Key words
• compound — the open ground around a house or school
• drain — a channel that carries water away
• conserve — to use something carefully so that it is not wasted
• environment — the air, water, land, plants and animals around us

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these words: brush, water, sweep, grass, lawn, bring.

Working:
1. Group /ʌ/, /ɔː/ and the clusters.
2. Brush has /ʌ/ and br. Water and lawn have /ɔː/. Sweep has sw. Grass and bring have gr and br.

Answer: /ʌ/: brush. /ɔː/: water, lawn. br: brush, bring. sw: sweep. gr: grass.

### Example 2
Turn this statement into a yes or no question: The bin is full.

Working:
1. Move is before the subject.
2. Raise your voice slightly at the end.

Answer: Is the bin full?

## Activity: Hear it and answer
You will need: The oral text, Word cards for broom, sweep, protect, clear, grass, water, rubbish
1. Listen to the oral text and repeat it without stopping after every word.
2. Hold up a card when you hear that word.
3. In pairs, ask three yes or no questions using the cards, and answer in short sentences.
4. Say one sentence of your own that includes a cluster, for example: Please bring a broom and sweep the path.

## Practice
1. Which words have /ʌ/: rubbish, water, cup, lawn, brush?
2. Write one word for each cluster: br, sw, pr, cl, gr.
3. Answer: Do you clear the drain when it is blocked?
4. What does conserve water mean?

## Summary
• /ʌ/ is short, as in rubbish and brush. /ɔː/ is long, as in water and lawn.
• Clusters br, sw, pr, cl and gr have no vowel between the consonants.
• Yes or no questions can be answered with yes or no and a short verb.

### Answers to practice
1. rubbish, cup, brush
2. Examples: broom, sweep, protect, clear, grass.
3. Example: Yes, I do. or No, I do not.
4. To use water carefully and not waste it.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Fluent speeches and messages without words

LESSON 2: FLUENT SPEECHES AND MESSAGES WITHOUT WORDS
====================================================

## What you will learn
• Speak a short text at the right speed and with expression.
• Use gestures and facial expressions that match the message.
• Explain why fluency helps a listener.

Curriculum outcomes: b) use nonverbal cues appropriately for self- expression; d) promote the importance of fluency in speech

## Introduction
A learner who says 'The... um... drain... is... um... blocked' makes the listener work too hard. The same fact, spoken in two smooth groups, is easier to act on: 'The drain is blocked. Please bring a broom.'

## Notes
### What fluency means
Fluent speech is accurate, expressive and steady. Accurate means the sounds and words are right. Expressive means your voice shows feeling and importance. Steady means you move at a speed others can follow, with only short pauses. A little hesitation while you think is normal. Long gaps filled with 'um' break the message.

Group words that belong together. 'Clear the drain / beside the kitchen / before the rain.' Pause at the slashes, not after every word.

### The right speed
If you speak too fast, listeners miss whether you said bin or bush, or grass or glass. If you speak too slowly, they forget the beginning before you reach the end. Practise by repeating a short text after your teacher or a recording until you can say it once without a stumble.

Try this: 'Our class cares for the compound. We sweep the paths, clear the drains and water the young trees. A clean neighbourhood is safer for everyone.'

### Messages without words
You can support speech, or sometimes replace a word, with nonverbal cues.

- Point to the bin when you say bin.
- Hold up a broom when you ask for one.
- Shake your head at litter on the grass.
- A worried face shows that a blocked drain matters.
- A smile and a nod thank someone who has helped.

The cue must match the words. Smiling while you describe a dangerous, flooded drain confuses people. If you pass a message with no words at all, choose a gesture the group has agreed on, and check that they understood.

### Why fluency matters
A fluent speaker is easier to trust and easier to follow. In a clean-up, people need instructions they can hear the first time. Fluency also shows respect: you have prepared, so you do not waste the listeners' time. The same skill helps every time you present work in class.

## Key words
• fluency — speech that is clear, expressive and steady, with little hesitation
• expression — the feeling and emphasis you put into your voice
• hesitation — an unwanted pause while you search for the next word
• nonverbal cue — a message from the face, hands or body

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Mark sensible pauses: Please sweep the path and empty the bin before lunch.

Working:
1. Keep phrases that belong together.
2. Do not pause after every word.

Answer: Please sweep the path / and empty the bin / before lunch.

### Example 2
Which gesture matches the sentence 'Put the rubbish in the bin'?

Working:
1. The important object is the bin.
2. Pointing to it supports the words.

Answer: Point to the bin, or mime dropping rubbish into it.

## Activity: A short speech on a clean place
You will need: The model text in the notes, A broom, a bin or pictures of them
1. Repeat the model text after the teacher until the group can say it with almost no hesitation.
2. In pairs, recite a short poem about the environment, keeping a steady rhythm and listening to each other's ideas with respect.
3. Prepare a short speech: name one dirty place, say what you will do, and say why it matters. Speak at a steady speed.
4. Add two nonverbal cues. The class says what those cues meant.

## Practice
1. What three things make speech fluent?
2. Why is speaking too fast a problem?
3. Give one way to pass a message without words.
4. Why does fluency matter during a clean-up?

## Summary
• Speak in phrases, at a speed listeners can follow.
• Let your face and hands match the words.
• Fluent instructions are easier and more respectful to follow.

### Answers to practice
1. Accuracy, expression and the right speed, with little hesitation.
2. Listeners may miss important words and not know what to do.
3. Example: Point to the bin, shake your head at litter, or mime using a broom.
4. People can follow the instructions the first time and work safely together.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 12.1.1 LISTENING AND SPEAKING: PRONUNCIATION AND VOCABULARY
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which word has the short sound /ʌ/?
   A. water
   B. lawn
   C. rubbish
   D. floor

2. Which word has the long sound /ɔː/?
   A. brush
   B. cup
   C. water
   D. sweep

3. Which word begins with the cluster sw?
   A. sweep
   B. grass
   C. protect
   D. clear

4. Which word begins with the cluster gr?
   A. broom
   B. grass
   C. clear
   D. protect

5. A drain is
   A. a channel that carries water away
   B. a kind of tree
   C. a game
   D. a colour

6. Which question can be answered with yes or no?
   A. Is the compound clean?
   B. What is a bin?
   C. Why do we plant trees?
   D. How do you make a broom?

7. Fluent speech is best described as
   A. as fast as possible
   B. accurate, expressive and steady
   C. full of long um sounds
   D. spoken one letter at a time

8. Which gesture best matches 'Put the paper in the bin'?
   A. Point to the bin
   B. Close your eyes and turn away
   C. Wave at the hills only
   D. Hide the broom

9. Why should you speak at the right speed?

10. Why is fluency important when you give a speech?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 12.1.1 LISTENING AND SPEAKING: PRONUNCIATION AND VOCABULARY
========================================

1. C. rubbish
   Rubbish has the short vowel /ʌ/. Water, lawn and floor have /ɔː/.

2. C. water
   Water has the long rounded sound /ɔː/.

3. A. sweep
   Sweep begins with s and w together.

4. B. grass
   Grass begins with g and r together.

5. A. a channel that carries water away
   A drain carries water away from a place.

6. A. Is the compound clean?
   Is the compound clean? can be answered yes or no.

7. B. accurate, expressive and steady
   Fluency is clear, expressive speech at a followable speed.

8. A. Point to the bin
   Pointing to the bin supports the instruction.

9. So listeners can hear each important word and remember the message.
   Too fast hides words. Too slow breaks the message apart.

10. Listeners can follow you the first time, and you show respect for their time.
   Fluent speech makes the message clear and considerate.
